title: Data in Software – Codebooks, Entry, Cleaning and an R Primer

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A codebook (data dictionary) lists every variable in a dataset with its name, label, type, unit, allowed values or range, codes for categories, and codes for missing values. Data entry is the transfer of recorded values into a computer file, ideally through a form that checks each value as it is entered. Data cleaning is the systematic search for, and correction of, errors before analysis: values out of range, inconsistent combinations, duplicates and missing values. A data frame is a table held by software, with one row per unit and one column per variable (§1.1).

The codebook, entry and cleaning habits below apply whatever software you use, from Epi Info or Excel to SPSS, Stata or R. The R primer at the end of this section (the In R (optional) box) is optional: if you will not use R, skip it. No later chapter needs it.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Every statistic in this book is only as good as the file it is computed from. Four habits protect that file.

  1. Write the codebook first. Short, lower-case variable names without spaces (weight_kg, not Weight of child (kg)); the unit in the name or label; one column per variable; one row per unit.
  2. Code missing values as missing. Leave the cell empty (read as NA in R). A code such as 999 is a number, and software will average it with the real weights unless told otherwise. Distinguish “not applicable” (a child not seen today has no arrival order) from “not recorded”.
  3. Enter through validating forms. Mobile tools such as Epicollect5, KoboToolbox and ODK let you set a range (weight 5–20 kg for this clinic), a type (number, date) and skip rules, so impossible values are refused in the field. For paper forms, double data entry (two people enter the same forms independently, then a program lists every cell where they disagree) catches any typing error that only one of the two people made.
  4. Clean with checks, not with your eyes. Range checks, consistency checks (a child marked “not seen today” should have no arrival order), duplicate IDs, and a count of missing values in every column. Keep the raw file untouched and do all corrections in a script, so every change is recorded.

Software differs in menus, not in logic. In SPSS you set a variable’s level (nominal, ordinal, scale) and its missing-value codes in Variable View; in Epi Info the form designer holds the ranges and legal values. In R you tell the software the scale by storing a categorical variable as a factor, and an ordinal one as an ordered factor (recall §1.1.2).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Codebook for the clinic register (data/clinic_children.csv, 100 rows):

Variable Label Type (scale) Values / range Missing
child_id Child ID text (identifier) C001–C100, unique none allowed
seen_today One of today’s 30 binary (nominal) 1 = yes, 0 = no none allowed
arrival_order Order of arrival today discrete (ordinal rank) 1–30 empty if seen_today = 0 (not applicable)
age_months Age continuous (ratio), recorded in completed months 12–36 empty
sex Sex nominal F, M empty
weight_kg Weight continuous (ratio) 5–20 kg, 0.1 kg precision empty
height_cm Length/height continuous (ratio) 65–110 cm empty
nutritional_status Nutritional status ordinal normal < moderate wasting < severe wasting empty
diarrhoea_episodes_month Diarrhoeal episodes, past month discrete (ratio) 0–10 empty
wealth_quintile Household wealth quintile ordinal 1 (poorest) – 5 empty
maternal_education Mother’s education ordinal none < primary < secondary+ empty

The ranges are the ones set for this clinic’s form; they are there to catch keying errors, not to define normal growth.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Suppose the last three children of the day were not weighed and their weights were keyed as 999 instead of left empty.

  1. Sum of the 27 real weights = 315.5 kg.
  2. Sum with the codes = 315.5 + 3 × 999 = 3,312.5.
  3. “Mean” over 30 = 3,312.5 ÷ 30 = 110.42 kg.
  4. Correct handling: mean of the 27 recorded weights = 315.5 ÷ 27 = 11.69 kg, reported with “weight missing for 3 children”.

Result: three missing-value codes turned an 11.7-kg mean into 110.4 kg. A range check (5–20 kg) flags all three at once. A subtler code (say 0.0) would drag the mean down without looking impossible, which is why missing values should be empty cells, not numbers. What to do about missing values in analysis is taken up in §15.4.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
Optional R primer: skip this box if you will not use R. R is free software for statistical computing (R Core Team, 2024); the output below comes from R 4.3.3. The lines below read the clinic register, tell R which variable is ordinal, and run the cleaning checks from the Simplified Explanation.

cl <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
dim(cl)
vars <- c("child_id", "sex", "weight_kg", "nutritional_status",
          "arrival_order")
str(cl[, vars])
cl$nutritional_status <- factor(cl$nutritional_status,
    levels = c("normal", "moderate wasting", "severe wasting"),
    ordered = TRUE)
table(cl$nutritional_status)
summary(cl$weight_kg)
range(cl$weight_kg)
sum(duplicated(cl$child_id))
colSums(is.na(cl))[c("weight_kg", "arrival_order")]
table(seen_today = cl$seen_today,
      has_order = !is.na(cl$arrival_order))
t30 <- subset(cl, seen_today == 1)
table(cut(t30$weight_kg, breaks = c(8, 10, 12, 14, 16),
          right = FALSE))

dim shows 100 rows (children) and 11 columns (variables). str shows each column’s type: chr is text, num a continuous number, int a whole number; nutritional_status arrives as plain text until factor(..., ordered = TRUE) records its order, after which table lists the categories in clinical order: 60 normal, 25 moderate and 15 severe wasting. summary gives the minimum (8.6 kg), maximum (15.4 kg), mean (12.15 kg) and three cut points you will meet as the quartiles and median (§2.3, §3.4). The checks pass: every weight lies inside 5–20 kg, no ID is duplicated, weight has no missing values, and the 70 missing arrival orders are exactly the 70 children not seen today (not applicable, not lost). The last table rebuilds §1.4.1 from the file: [8,10) is R’s notation for “8 to <10”, and right = FALSE is what puts the 10.0-kg child in the second class.

points.html: Codebook before data collection; one row per unit, one column per variable; names without spaces.
Missing values are empty cells (NA), never 0, 99 or 999. Separate “not applicable” from “not recorded”.
Prevent errors at entry (validating forms, double entry); detect the rest with scripted range, consistency, duplicate and missing-value checks.
Never overwrite the raw file; correct in a script that can be rerun.
Declare each variable’s scale in the software, so that it respects the scale (§1.1.2). In R (optional), that means storing nominal variables as factors and ordinal variables as ordered factors.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 1.7

questions.prompt: Write codebook rows (name, type, values, missing code) for “ever breastfed (yes/no)” and “age at first solid food in months” in an infant-feeding survey.
questions.answer:
Variable Label Type (scale) Values / range Missing
ever_bf Ever breastfed binary (nominal) 1 = yes, 0 = no empty cell
age_solids_mo Age at first solid food continuous (ratio), recorded in completed months 0–24 months empty if not recorded; “not yet started” (not applicable) recorded in a separate variable (e.g. solids_started = 1 yes / 0 no), never as 0 or a code in this column

questions.prompt: In a double-entry comparison of 250 forms with 40 fields each, 30 cells disagree. What percentage of cells disagree, and what do you do with each disagreeing cell?
questions.answer: Cells = 250 × 40 = 10,000. Disagreement = 30 ÷ 10,000 = 0.3%. For each of the 30 cells, pull the original paper form, read the true value, and correct whichever entry is wrong, recording the correction in the cleaning log or script. Cells where both typists made the same error are not caught, which is why range and consistency checks follow.

questions.prompt: (Optional, R) Why does table(cl$nutritional_status) list “moderate wasting” first if you skip the factor(...) line? (Hint: without levels, R sorts text alphabetically.)
questions.answer: Without the factor(..., levels = ..., ordered = TRUE) line, the column is plain text, and R sorts text alphabetically: “moderate wasting” < “normal” < “severe wasting”. The clinical order (normal < moderate < severe) exists only in your head until you declare it as an ordered factor.
